samples.summary: Folder delete authorization is checked only on the target folder, but the delete cascades to descendant folders authored by other members
samples.evidence: `remove()` gates on `isManager(folder, req)` for the *named* folder only (folders.controller.ts:148), then calls `folderService.delete(folderId)` → `prisma.folder.delete({where:{id}})` (folder.service.ts:44). `Folder.parent` is declared `onDelete: Cascade` on the self-relation (packages/backend/prisma/schema.prisma:137), so the DB removes the whole subtree. A plain member who authored folder F is a manager of F only, yet deleting F destroys every descendant folder — including ones authored by the workspace owner or other members, whose documents are then re-parented to the workspace root via `Document.folder onDelete: SetNull` (schema.prisma:123). Attack: member M creates F; any manager who nests their own folder G under F (a legitimate move M cannot perform, so the escalation requires the victim to nest voluntarily) loses G and every folder beneath it when M calls `DELETE /api/v1/workspaces/:wid/folders/F`. The same non-recursive check exists on the pre-existing web route (folder.controller.ts:113), so this change replicates rather than introduces the gap — but it newly makes it reachable with a `write`-scoped API key, i.e. from unattended automation. Consider asserting manager authority over the subtree (or refusing to delete a folder that has descendants the caller does not manage).

samples.summary: `PATCH /api/v1/.../documents/:id` accepts an unvalidated inline body, so neither `title` nor the new `folderId` gets the DTO validation the web route and the sibling folders controller apply
samples.evidence: The handler declares `@Body() body: { title?: string; folderId?: string | null }` — a TypeScript inline type, whose emitted `design:paramtypes` metatype is `Object`. Nest's global `ValidationPipe` (packages/backend/src/main.ts:65-72, configured `whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true`) short-circuits for the `Object` metatype, so *no* validation or whitelisting runs on this route. The web equivalent uses `UpdateDocumentDto` with `@IsString() @Length(1,200)` on `title` and `@IsUUID()` on `folderId` (packages/backend/src/document/document.dto.ts:92-106), and the new `ApiV1FoldersController` correctly uses `CreateFolderDto`/`UpdateFolderDto` (packages/backend/src/folder/folder.dto.ts). Consequences: (a) `data.title = body.title` (documents.controller.ts:123) writes an arbitrarily long / non-string value — bounded only by the 25MB JSON body cap (main.ts:20) — letting any member or write-scoped key bloat the `Document.title` column repeatedly; (b) a non-string `folderId` (array/object) reaches `folderService.assertSameWorkspace` → `prisma.folder.findUnique({where:{id: <object>}})` and surfaces as an unhandled Prisma validation error rather than a 400. I could not build an authorization bypass from it: `assertSameWorkspace` gates the `connect` and `data` is assembled field-by-field, so the pre-existing mass-assignment exposure (the old `data: body`, which could have carried `workspace: {connect:{id}}`) is actually closed by this change. Recommend reusing a real DTO here.
searchedFor: read packages/backend/src/main.ts for useGlobalPipes / ValidationPipe options
grep 'data: body|\.\.\.body' across packages/backend/src (no remaining mass-assignment sites)

samples.summary: `POST /documents/:id/copy` is membership-gated with no dedicated throttle, so a write-scoped key can amplify storage/CPU at the global 120 req/min budget
samples.evidence: `copy()` runs `DocumentCopyService.copy` (documents.controller.ts:107), which for `pdf`/`image`/`file` documents performs a server-side blob `CopyObject` (document-copy.service.ts:198) and for CRDT types snapshots and rewrites a whole Yorkie root. The gate is workspace membership only (deliberate, and matching the web route). Only the global `ThrottlerModule.forRoot` bucket applies (app.module.ts:97; default 120/60s) — sibling blob-touching v1 controllers set explicit `@Throttle` (files.controller.ts:53, images.controller.ts:23) and the copy engine's other member-reachable caller bounds itself with `MAX_REHOSTED_IMAGES`/`MAX_REHOSTED_BYTES`. Result: a single write-scoped key can duplicate a near-cap blob document ~120×/min with no per-caller quota. The web `POST documents/:id/copy` has the same exposure (no `@Throttle` in document.controller.ts), so this is parity rather than a regression — but the API-key surface exists specifically for unattended automation, which makes the missing bound more consequential here.

finding.summary: API-key branch of the image read route still skips the minter-membership check, so the new "a key does not outlive its minter's membership" invariant does not hold for the whole /api/v1 surface as the docs now claim
finding.evidence: This delta's whole premise is that an API key is resolved to `apiKey.createdBy` and re-checked against that user's *current* membership (`workspace-scope.guard.ts:38`), and docs/design/rest-api.md:509-513 now states `WorkspaceScopeGuard` "enforces the removal half for the **whole** v1 surface" so that "removing somebody from a workspace revokes the keys they minted". `ApiV1ImageReadController` is on that surface (`@Controller('api/v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/images')`, image-read.controller.ts:40) but mounts only `OptionalCombinedAuthGuard` (line 41) — not `WorkspaceScopeGuard` — and its own gate short-circuits on `if (user?.isApiKey) { if (user.workspaceId === resolvedWorkspaceId) return; }` (lines 96-97), never touching `assertMember` and never looking at `user.id`. Attack: an owner mints a key, is then removed from the workspace (`WorkspaceService.removeMember`, workspace.service.ts:94). Every mutating/reading v1 route now 403s for that key, but `GET /api/v1/workspaces/:wid/images/:imageId` still streams any workspace image blob to the holder of the ex-member's key (image ids are learnable from any document content the key holder captured earlier, or from a share link). The gate reads as covered surface-wide when one read path is not.

verdict.reason: The quoted vulnerable code does not exist. `ApiV1ImageReadController.assertCanRead` does NOT short-circuit on the API-key branch: after the scope check (image-read.controller.ts:98-100) it awaits `this.workspaceService.assertMember(resolvedWorkspaceId, Number(user.id))` (lines 108-111) before returning. `user.id` is the minter (`apiKey.createdBy`, api-key.strategy.ts:23), and `assertMember` (workspace.service.ts:236-243) reads the current `workspaceMember` row, so a removed minter's key gets a ForbiddenException — the same bar as WorkspaceScopeGuard:40-44. The key branch throws/returns before the `?token=` fallback, so there is no share-token laundering path. `WorkspaceService.removeMember` additionally revokes the minted key rows transactionally (workspace.service.ts:109-114). Specs pin both behaviors: image-read.controller.spec.ts:164-188 (assertMember called with ('w1',7)) and :190-218 (removed minter forbidden, findByToken never called). The only sibling route on the same path prefix is the write controller, which mounts CombinedAuthGuard + WorkspaceScopeGuard + ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard (images.controller.ts:22). The claimed hole in the "key does not outlive its minter's membership" invariant is not present.

finding.summary: Member removal still never revokes ApiKey rows; the new membership check only suspends a key, so re-adding the user silently reactivates every key they ever minted (docs claim removal "revokes" them)
finding.evidence: The delta deliberately substitutes a live membership lookup for key revocation — workspace-scope.guard.ts:14-20 and docs/design/rest-api.md:509-513 say this makes removal "revoke the keys they minted without a key-sweep on the member-removal path". But `removeMember` (workspace.service.ts:94-112) only deletes the `WorkspaceMember` row; `ApiKey.revokedAt` is untouched (no `apiKey` reference anywhere under src/workspace), and `ApiKey` has no relation to `WorkspaceMember` (schema.prisma:209-223, key hangs off `workspaceId` + `createdBy`), so nothing cascades. The keys therefore stay valid rows that authenticate successfully (`ApiKeyService.validateKey` checks only revokedAt/expiresAt, api-key.service.ts:65-93) and are merely denied at the membership gate. If the ex-member is later re-invited — `acceptInvite` re-creates the membership with the invite's role, workspace.service.ts:152-178, and a plain-`member` invite is enough — every previously issued key (including one leaked while the person was gone) starts working again with write scope and member authority (create documents, destructive `PUT .../content`), with no operator action and no visibility. Removal is a suspension, not a revocation; the honest fix is to set `revokedAt` on the removed user's keys for that workspace in `removeMember` (the membership check remains a useful belt-and-braces).

verdict.reason: The claim is that `removeMember` never revokes ApiKey rows, leaving keys that reactivate on re-invite. The counterexample is in the exact function named: workspace.service.ts:115-124 wraps the membership delete and `tx.apiKey.updateMany({ where: { workspaceId, createdBy: targetUserId, revokedAt: null }, data: { revokedAt: new Date() } })` in a single `$transaction`. The where-clause fields match the real schema (ApiKey.workspaceId String at schema.prisma:214, createdBy Int at :216, revokedAt at :221), and `revokedAt` is precisely the field ApiKeyService.validateKey rejects on (api-key.service.ts:76) — so the swept keys are dead at authentication, not merely denied at the membership gate. Because revokedAt is persisted at removal time and acceptInvite performs no apiKey write, a later re-invite cannot resurrect them. Tests pin the behavior (workspace.service.spec.ts:322-339 asserts the updateMany args and that $transaction was used), and the guard's own comment (workspace-scope.guard.ts:19-22) describes itself as the "live half" complementing this outright revocation. The asserted absence does not exist in this working tree.
